blocks.md: This lesson follows **Attention State as a Serving Resource** in *KV Cache Management* (Vol III).

blocks.source: Vol III, KV Cache Management, § Attention State as a Serving Resource
blocks.md: The connection-pool repair agent (a later section) has reached a candidate revision, r18. Its targeted reproducer passes, prompting the harness to submit a fully serialized request of 32,768 tokens and launch an integration test suite that runs for 45 seconds. If the serving engine holds the request's attention state in accelerator memory throughout that entire wait, the device does no work for that workflow. The model generates zero tokens during the test suite, yet its retained state pins memory that another concurrent request could put to work.

questions.q: The section **Attention State as a Serving Resource** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Retained attention state costs 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes per token, so resident fit in the KV pool falls as 1/S with context length, and the attention design fixed at pretraining sets the slope.

A content-keyed radix tree finds the longest retained common prefix, leaf-first eviction keeps residency prefix-closed, and efficacy is the token-weighted hit rate after availability, permission, and block rounding.
Mean occupancy equals arrival rate times mean residence (L = lambda W), a mean identity that sizes slot pools but says nothing about peaks.
Splitting an uncached prompt into chunks under a per-iteration token budget bounds the inter-token gap of ongoing streams to one iteration at a modest delay to the new request's first token.
